 NECESSITY FOR THE BELL COUNTY                        §
 EAST SWITCH TO BIG HILL SUBSTATION                   §
 765-KV TRANSMISSION LINE PROJECT IN                  §
 BELL, BURNET, CONCHO, CORYELL,                       §
 LAMPASAS,       LLANO,      MASON,                   §
 MCCULLOCH, MENARD, MILAM, MILLS,                     §
 SAN SABA, SCHLEICHER, TOM GREEN,                     §
 AND WILLIAMSON COUNTIES                              §

                FLEMING SPRINGS RANCH LAND COMPANY, LLC’S
               REPLY TO EXCEPTIONS TO PROPOSAL FOR DECISION

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

       Intervenor Fleming Springs Ranch Land Company, LLC (“Fleming Springs”) respectfully

files its Reply to Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision issued in this Docket on August 20, 2026

("PFD"), and would respectfully show:

I.     Issues and Exceptions Addressed

       If the Commission approves the Application and selects a route, Fleming Springs supports

the ALJs’ recommendation of Route 894 as the route that best meets the relevant routing criteria.

       Fleming Springs responds to exceptions to the PFD, including those of the Solana

Intervenors (“Solana”) [Item 6467]; Brady Creek Intervenors (“BCI”) [Item 6468]; and 4K Land

and Cattle Company (“4K Land”) [Item 6478]. These exceptions raise several due process

arguments that Fleming Springs does not address. Instead, Fleming Springs limits its response to

routing analysis and its opposition to northern corridor routes, including Routes 392 and 410.




FLEMING SPRINGS REPLY TO EXCEPTIONS TO PROPOSAL FOR DECISION                               PAGE 1
         The PFD's findings and recommendation to select Route 894 are supported by a

preponderance of the record evidence, and the exceptions do not establish any error in the ALJs’

evaluation of cost, community values, landowner impacts, prudent avoidance, or environmental

performance. If the Commission reaches route selection, it should overrule the exceptions and

adopt Route 894.

II.     Argument

        A.       Prudent Avoidance; 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(iv)

        Under 16 TAC § 25.101, the Commission is required to follow the policy of prudent

avoidance, which is defined as the “limiting of exposures to electric and magnetic fields that can

be avoided with reasonable investments of money and effort.” 1 Applied here, this principle

requires minimizing the number of habitable structures affected by the transmission line while

avoiding unnecessary or inefficient costs.

        The northern corridor supporters argue that the number of habitable structures is merely a

proxy and should not be treated as determinative. 2 Fleming Springs agrees that prudent avoidance

is not determined by a simple tally of habitable structures and instead requires consideration of all

relevant routing criteria. Yet Route 894 remains the strongest performer under that broader

analysis. Recognizing habitable structure impacts as only one factor in the analysis does not lessen

Route 894's advantage. Rather, it reflects the balanced approach adopted by the ALJs and supports

their conclusion that Route 894 provides the most reasonable overall route.

        Route 894 would place 85 habitable structures within 500 feet of the centerline, the third

fewest among all filed routes. 3 There is no route in this proceeding that costs less than Route 894



1
  16 TAC §25.101(a)(6)
2
  Solana Exceptions at 14; see also 4K Land Exceptions at 23-24.
3
  Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 23 (Combined Data Table).

FLEMING SPRINGS REPLY TO EXCEPTIONS TO PROPOSAL FOR DECISION                                 PAGE 2
 while also impacting the same number of habitable structures or fewer. Every route with fewer or

equal structures costs more. Every route that costs less has more habitable structures.

        Route 392, by contrast, places 136 habitable structures within 500 feet of its centerline, 51

more than Route 894, 44 of which are single-family residences. 4 This impact translates to 44

additional homes and families being placed within 500 feet of one of Texas's highest-voltage

transmission lines. 5

        The PFD shows that the ALJs performed a balancing analysis of Route 894 and found it

achieved prudent avoidance more effectively than the northern routes, which ran through or

adjacent to more habitable structures at a higher cost to the ratepayers. The ALJs specifically called

out that Route 392 has notably more habitable structures and cultural resources than the other

Focus Routes. 6

        Recognizing that Route 392 does not satisfy the prudent avoidance principle, proponents

of the northern routes have advanced Route 410 as an alternative that preserves Route 392’s alleged

paralleling advantages while addressing the ALJs’ concerns regarding impacts on habitable

structures.

        Route 410 would place 98 habitable structures within 500 feet of the centerline, 13 more

than Route 894. 7 BCI attempts to argue that the difference "doesn't offer much if anything in the

way of a basis for a decision between Route 894 and Route 410," and then pivots to paralleling. 8

        Route 410 is more expensive than each of the four major Focus Routes considered in this

proceeding, including Route 392, the route it is offered to replace. 9 Route 410's estimated cost is


4
   Hodge/Schwertner et al. Ex. 2 (Cross-rebuttal Testimony of Brian C. Andrews.) at 9-10.
5
  PFD at 143-144.
6
  Id. at 147.
7
  Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 23 (Combined Data Table).
8
  BCI Exceptions at 31.
9
  PFD at 16.

FLEMING SPRINGS REPLY TO EXCEPTIONS TO PROPOSAL FOR DECISION                                  PAGE 3
 almost $57 million more than Route 894.10 A route that is longer, more expensive, and impacts

more homes than Route 894 does not remedy the prudent-avoidance shortcomings of Route 392.

It merely shifts the tradeoff without producing a better outcome than Route 894.

        Route 410 is therefore not a compromise that improves on Route 894; it is a more expensive

route that burdens more homes for a benefit the record does not support. The ALJs correctly found

that Route 894 "complies with the Commission's policy of prudent avoidance" 11 and achieves that

policy "more effectively" than the northern corridor alternatives. 12 No party has identified a route

that places fewer homes near this 765-kV line at a lower cost, and neither Route 392 nor Route

410 does so. If the Commission reaches route selection, prudent avoidance points squarely to

Route 894.

        B.         Paralleling and the Colorado River Crossing; 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(i)-(iii)

        BCI, Solana, and 4K Land all press a recalculated "hard paralleling" metric under which

Route 392 parallels 41 miles of transmission lines, roads, and railroads against only 10.1 miles for

Route 894. 13 They reach that figure by discarding parallels of apparent property boundaries as

"unreliable." 14

        That approach cannot be squared with the Commission's rule. Rule 25.101(b)(3)(B) lists

three co-equal paralleling subfactors, the third of which is "whether the routes parallel property

lines or other natural or cultural features." Paralleling property lines is not a lesser form of

paralleling. It is one of the categories expressly recognized by the rule and helps reduce impacts

on landowners by following existing property boundaries rather than bisecting tracts.



10
   Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 23 (Combined Data Table).
11
   PFD at 184, FOF 167-168.
12
   Id. at 147.
13
   BCI Exhibit 61
14
   BCI Exceptions at 30.

FLEMING SPRINGS REPLY TO EXCEPTIONS TO PROPOSAL FOR DECISION                                 PAGE 4
         Even if the Commission credits the hard-paralleling advantages emphasized by proponents

of the northern corridor routes, the customary benefits of paralleling provide little support for those

routes here.

        The northern corridor route supporters argue that Route 392’s use of Link U3, which

crosses the Colorado River parallel to an existing transmission line, makes it the best location to

cross the River. Fleming Springs does not dispute that the Colorado River crossing is a significant

component of the project. However, this argument overstates the benefits that Link U3 actually

offers, because the advantage of running alongside an existing line depends on the two lines being

alike; the line at Link U3 and this proposed 765-kV line are not.

        The existing line is adjacent to Fleming Springs Ranch and discussed in Ms. Jones’s direct

testimony.15 It is roughly 65 feet tall. 16 Applicants’ proposed structures will be 140-170 feet tall,

potentially up to 198 feet tall. 17 As part of her direct testimony, Ms. Jones photographed the

landscape at the location of the existing line from a helicopter at both heights, and the difference

is marked. Excerpts from her testimony showing those photos are below.




15
   Fleming Springs Ranch Ex. 1, pp. 13-15.
16
   Id.
17
   Applicants’ Ex. 1, p. 67.

FLEMING SPRINGS REPLY TO EXCEPTIONS TO PROPOSAL FOR DECISION                                   PAGE 5
        A 765-kV transmission line demands a substantially wider right-of-way corridor than

lower-voltage lines due to its larger structures and the increased clearances required for safe

operation. This project will require acquisition of new, independent right-of-way along its corridor,

even if it parallels in part the existing line. This further diminishes the apparent value of Link U3’s

paralleling.




FLEMING SPRINGS REPLY TO EXCEPTIONS TO PROPOSAL FOR DECISION                                   PAGE 6
         The benefits of paralleling would be in minimizing environmental disturbance, land

fragmentation, and impacts on landowners. This would apply if a new line can share an existing

disturbed corridor. In this case, those benefits do not exist, because the necessary clearances and

structure footprints of the enormous new line will require the creation of a substantially new and

independent corridor, even when placed near existing infrastructure.

        C.       Costs; 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)

        BCI, Solana, and 4K Land dismiss the $34.3 million gap between Route 894 and Route

392, and the $56.5 million gap between Route 894 and Route 410, 18 citing the 10–15% cost

contingency range testified at the hearing. 19 Taken to its logical conclusion, that argument would

eliminate cost as a distinguishing factor in every transmission line proceeding in Texas, since all

preliminary estimates inherently involve some uncertainty. The cost analysis rests on the same data

and cuts the same way.

        The cost estimates for this project were prepared using the same methodology and applied

uniformly across all 122 filed routes. The cost contingency affects all routes proportionally; it does

not selectively impact Route 392 or Route 410’s costs but not Route 894’s. As expert Brian C.

Andrews explained in his cross-rebuttal testimony, tariffs and cost escalation factors are

multiplicative, not selective. 20 Any potential increase in costs, whether due to tariffs, material

escalation, or contingency realization, applies proportionally to all routes.

        Longer routes are going to be more expensive. Their contingencies are proportionate to

their increased costs, and their uncertainties are proportionate to their increased costs. Route 392

is almost 6 miles and Route 410 is over 10 miles longer than Route 894.



18
   BCI Exceptions at 32. 4K Land Exceptions at 23-24.
19
   PFD at 129-130.
20
   Hodge/Schwertner et al. Ex. 2 (Cross-rebuttal Testimony of Brian C. Andrews.) at 16.

FLEMING SPRINGS REPLY TO EXCEPTIONS TO PROPOSAL FOR DECISION                                  PAGE 7
         D.       Environmental Factors

        As stated earlier, Fleming Springs does not dispute that the Colorado River crossing is a

significant component of the project. However, the northern corridor supporters only discuss the

Colorado River crossing at Link U3, where it parallels an existing transmission line, as the decisive

reason the Commission should select Route 392. 21 That contention disregards the environmental

consequences of Link U3’s impact on the Colorado River. At the hearing, there was significant

discussion about Ecologically Significant Stream Segment (ESSS) designations, assigned by the

Texas Parks and Wildlife Department. 22 The ESSS designation identifies river and stream

segments of particular ecological importance based on biological function, hydrologic function,

riparian conservation areas, high water quality and exceptional aquatic life, and the presence of

threatened or endangered species. 23

         Links U3, U2, and J11 are the three northernmost proposed Colorado River crossings

within the Study Area, and all three traverse the designated ESSS portion of the river, unlike the

southern crossings, which are not designated ESSS. 24 This data shows that selecting a Colorado

River crossing in this proceeding involves nuanced tradeoffs, requiring a balance between

environmental integrity and all other routing considerations.

E.      Best Route Alternative

        Route 894 protects cultural and environmental resources that would otherwise be placed at

risk, performs well with respect to prudent avoidance, and is the lowest-cost route that meets these

objectives. No competing route provides this combination. A side-by-side comparison of the data

shows that Route 392 or Route 410 cannot be considered superior to Route 894:

III.   Conclusion

       Therefore, Fleming Springs respectfully requests that, if the Commission grants the

Application; that it select Route 894 as the route that best meets the criteria of PURA § 37.056(c)(4)

and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B).
